title: The $500 Million Art Heist Still Unsolved

beats.say: In a museum in Boston, there are empty picture frames hanging on the walls. They've been empty for more than thirty five years. The paintings that belong in them were stolen in one night, and nobody has ever found them.
The thirteen stolen works are worth an estimated five hundred million dollars. It's often called the biggest art theft in history, and the most valuable unsolved property crime in the United States.

vis.label: estimated value of the stolen works
vis.source: Estimates of the 1990 Gardner Museum theft

beats.say: And there's a reward of ten million dollars for information that leads to the art coming home. Still unclaimed.
Part one. The museum.

The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum was created by a wealthy collector, Isabella Stewart Gardner, who filled a Venetian style palace in Boston with art from around the world. It opened to the public in nineteen oh three.

vis.sub: A palace of art in Boston

beats.say: Her will is said to have set a strict rule: the collection should stay arranged the way she left it. Which is one reason why, after the theft, the museum left the empty frames hanging. Waiting.

vis.text: The frames stay. Waiting for the paintings.

beats.say: Part two. The knock at the door.

In the early hours of the eighteenth of March, nineteen ninety, it was the night after St Patrick's Day in Boston. At about one twenty four in the morning, two men dressed as police officers came to the museum's side door.
They told the guard on duty that they were responding to a disturbance. And he buzzed them in. That broke the museum's rule never to let anyone in at night.

vis.who: the fake police officers at the museum door

beats.say: Once inside, the fake officers said they recognised one of the guards and had a warrant for his arrest. They handcuffed both guards, took them to the basement, and tied them up with tape.
Part three. Eighty one minutes.
Then the thieves had the museum to themselves. They spent around eighty one minutes inside.

They took a Vermeer, The Concert, one of only around three dozen paintings by Vermeer known in the world. They took Rembrandt's only known seascape, The Storm on the Sea of Galilee. They took a Manet, and works by Degas.

vis.title: What they took
items: Rembrandt, The Storm on the Sea of Galilee

beats.say: Some of the paintings were cut roughly out of their frames with a blade. For art experts, that was heartbreaking. Masterpieces hundreds of years old were treated like posters.

The choices were strange, too. The thieves walked past some of the most valuable works in the building, including a famous Titian. And they took odd items, like a bronze eagle from the top of a flagpole, and an ancient Chinese bronze cup.

Motion detectors in the museum recorded their footsteps, room by room. But oddly, the sensors showed no movement in one room where a stolen item had been. Mysteries like that have kept investigators guessing for decades.

vis.sub: Tracked them room by room, with gaps

beats.say: At around two forty five in the morning, the thieves left, in two trips, carrying hundreds of millions of dollars of art. The guards were found the next morning.
Think about that night from the guards' point of view. Two men in uniform arrive. You do what police tell you. That instinct to obey authority was the thieves' real key to the building.

vis.text: Their real key was a uniform.

beats.say: Part four. The investigation.

The FBI has followed thousands of leads. Theories have included local organised crime, the Irish Republican Army, and international art thieves. Even the guard who opened the door has faced questions, though he was never charged.

In twenty thirteen, the FBI said it believed it knew who the thieves were, members of a criminal organisation based in the eastern United States, and that both were dead. But it didn't name them publicly. And the art wasn't found.

vis.text: FBI says it believes it knows who stole the Gardner art
vis.date: But the paintings are still missing

beats.say: Over the years, investigators focused on people linked to organised crime, including an elderly mobster who denied knowing anything. The trail has led to dead ends again and again.

vis.text: Lead after lead. Dead end after dead end.

beats.say: Part five. Why steal art you can't sell?

vis.text: Why steal art you can't sell?

beats.say: Here's the money puzzle. Famous paintings are almost impossible to sell. Every museum, auction house and serious collector knows they're stolen. So why take them?

Experts think stolen art is sometimes used like a bargaining chip. Criminals may hold it as collateral in deals, or hope to trade it for a lighter prison sentence one day. In the criminal world, a masterpiece can be worth more as leverage than as art.

vis.title: What stolen art is used for

beats.say: And that's the strangest part of art theft. The thing that makes these paintings so valuable, the fact that everyone knows them, is exactly what makes them almost worthless to the people who stole them.
Somewhere, possibly, The Concert is sitting in a closet, an attic, or a crate. And in Boston, the frame is still on the wall, waiting for it to come home.
